summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived overview of the Somali people, covering the history of independence and the Somali Republic, Somali cinema, Islam in Somalia, ancient history and rock art, medieval Somali sultanates, language and demographics, the diaspora, Qur'anic education, Djibouti's referendum, the Somali flag, genetics, and the origin of the name Somali. It frames Somalis as an ethnic group concentrated in the Horn of Africa, predominantly Sunni Muslim, with a large diaspora.
one_line: An overview of the Somali people's history, religion, language, culture, film, demographics and diaspora across the Horn of Africa.
key_facts: British Somaliland became independent on 26 June 1960 as the State of Somaliland, and the Trust Territory of Somalia followed five days later.
On 1 July 1960, the two territories united to form the Somali Republic, within boundaries drawn up by Italy and Britain.
Abdirashid Ali Shermarke served as Prime Minister and later as President from 1967 to 1969.
The Somali Film Agency (SFA) regulatory body was created in 1975, after which the local film scene began to expand rapidly.
The Somali flag was created in 1954 by the Somali scholar Mohammed Awale Liban and adopted as the national flag upon independence in 1960.
Somalis are predominantly Sunni Muslim, mostly belonging to the Shafi`i school of Islamic jurisprudence, although a few are Shia.
Laas Geel is a rock art complex in northern Somalia containing some of the earliest known rock art on the African continent.
Ethnic Somalis number around 16-20 million, with about 12.3 million in Somalia, 4.6 million in Ethiopia, 2.4 million in Kenya and 464,600 in Djibouti.
Somalis constitute approximately 85% of the population of Somalia.
An official 2010 estimate reported 108,000 Somalis living in the United Kingdom, with London accounting for roughly 78% of Britain's Somali population.
In 1975, the Somali Democratic Republic's Family Law put women and men on complete equal footing, including equal division of property upon divorce.

The Dervish State led by Mohammed Abdullah Hassan repulsed the British empire four times, and the Dervishes were finally defeated in 1920 when Britain bombed the Dervish capital of Taleex with airplanes.
In 1958 a referendum in Djibouti (then French Somaliland) resulted in continued association with France, largely due to a yes vote by the Afar ethnic group and resident Europeans.
Hassan Gouled Aptidon, who campaigned for a yes vote in the 1958 referendum, became Djibouti's first president (1977–1991).
The name Somali is generally regarded as deriving from Irir Samaale, the oldest common ancestor of several Somali clans, and is held to derive from soo and maal meaning 'go and milk'.
